title: AC Circuits
subject: Physics
subtitle: Class 12 HSC & MHT-CET • Rapid Revision Deck

cards.q: RMS value and Average value of an alternating current i = i₀ sin(ω t)?
cards.a:
RMS Value (Virtual value): I_rms = i₀ / √2 ≈ 0.707 i₀
Average Value (over positive half-cycle): I_avg = 2 i₀ / π ≈ 0.637 i₀.
Average value over a complete full cycle is strictly ZERO.
cards.hint: Household AC 220 V is the RMS voltage (e_rms = 220 V); peak voltage is e₀ = 220 × √2 ≈ 311 V.

cards.q: Why do hot-wire AC ammeters and voltmeters measure RMS values instead of peak values?
cards.a: They operate on the HEATING effect of electric current (H ∝ I²). Heat produced by AC equals heat produced by steady DC of magnitude I_rms: H = I_rms² R t.
cards.hint: Ordinary moving coil DC meters read 0 for AC because average torque over a cycle is zero.

cards.q: AC through Pure Resistor (R): Phase relation and opposition?
cards.a:
Voltage and current are IN PHASE (phase difference ϕ = 0).
Opposition: Resistance R (independent of frequency f).
Average power consumed: P = e_rms · I_rms = e₀ i₀ / 2.
cards.hint: Phasors for voltage and current lie along the same line.

cards.q: AC through Pure Inductor (L): Phase relation and Inductive Reactance X_L?
cards.a:
Voltage LEADS current by 90° (π/2 rad), or current lags voltage by π/2.
Inductive Reactance: X_L = ω L = 2 π f L (SI unit: Ohm Ω).
Average power consumed over full cycle: P = 0.
cards.hint: For DC (f = 0): X_L = 0 (inductor offers zero reactance to DC). X_L increases linearly with frequency (X_L ∝ f).

cards.q: AC through Pure Capacitor (C): Phase relation and Capacitive Reactance X_C?
cards.a:
Current LEADS voltage by 90° (π/2 rad), or voltage lags current by π/2.
Capacitive Reactance: X_C = 1 / (ω C) = 1 / (2 π f C) (SI unit: Ohm Ω).
Average power consumed over full cycle: P = 0.
cards.hint: For DC (f = 0): X_C = ∞ (capacitor completely BLOCKS direct current). X_C decreases with frequency (X_C ∝ 1/f).

cards.q: Series LCR Circuit: Formula for Impedance Z and Phase angle ϕ?
cards.a:
Impedance: Z = √[ R² + (X_L - X_C)² ] = √[ R² + (ω L - 1/(ω C))² ].
Phase angle: tan ϕ = (X_L - X_C) / R.
RMS current: I_rms = e_rms / Z.
cards.hint: If X_L > X_C: circuit is Inductive (voltage leads current). If X_C > X_L: circuit is Capacitive (current leads voltage).

cards.q: Condition for Electrical Resonance in a Series LCR circuit?
cards.a:
X_L = X_C ⇒ ω_r L = 1 / (ω_r C) ⇒ Resonant angular frequency: ω_r = 1 / √(L C).
Resonant frequency: f_r = 1 / [ 2π √(L C) ].
cards.hint: Inductive reactance exactly balances capacitive reactance, leaving the circuit purely resistive.

cards.q: Characteristics of a Series LCR Circuit at Resonance?
cards.a:
1. Impedance is MINIMUM and purely resistive: Z_min = R.
2. Current is MAXIMUM: I_max = e_rms / R.
3. Phase angle is ZERO (ϕ = 0): Voltage and current are in phase.
4. Power factor is MAXIMUM: cos ϕ = 1.
5. Called an ACCEPTOR CIRCUIT (used in radio tuning to select a specific frequency).
cards.hint: Board 3-mark favorite! Voltages across L and C cancel each other completely (V_L + V_C = 0).

cards.q: Parallel Resonance Circuit: Resonant frequency and properties?
cards.a:
Resonant frequency: f_r = (1 / 2π) √[ 1/(LC) - R²/(L²) ] ≈ 1 / [ 2π √(LC) ] (if R is small).
Characteristics: Impedance is MAXIMUM (Z_max = L / (C R)), Current is MINIMUM (I_min).
Called a REJECTOR CIRCUIT (filter circuit).
cards.hint: Opposite to series resonance! Series has minimum impedance; parallel has maximum impedance.

cards.q: Quality Factor (Q-Factor) of a series LCR resonant circuit?
cards.a: Q = ω_r L / R = 1 / (ω_r C R) = (1 / R) √(L / C) = f_r / Δf, where Δf is bandwidth (f₂ - f₁).
cards.hint: Dimensionless pure number. Higher Q-factor gives sharper, more selective resonance and smaller bandwidth.

cards.q: True Power, Apparent Power, and Power Factor in an AC circuit?
cards.a:
True Power: P = e_rms · I_rms · cos ϕ (in Watts W).
Apparent (Virtual) Power: P_app = e_rms · I_rms (in Volt-Amperes VA).
Power Factor: cos ϕ = True Power / Apparent Power = R / Z.
cards.hint: For pure R: cos ϕ = 1 (P = e_rms I_rms). For pure L or pure C: ϕ = 90° ⇒ cos ϕ = 0 (P = 0, zero power loss!).

cards.q: What is Wattless Current (Idle Current) in an AC circuit?
cards.a:
The component of alternating current that consumes ZERO average electric power: I_wattless = I_rms · sin ϕ.
Occurs when phase difference is ϕ = 90° (in a pure inductor or pure capacitor).
cards.hint: The current flows back and forth exchanging energy with the field without dissipating heat.

cards.q: Why is a Choke Coil preferred over a Rheostat for reducing AC current in tube lights?
cards.a:
A Choke Coil has high self-inductance L and negligible resistance R. It reduces AC current by offering high reactance (X_L = ωL) with nearly ZERO power dissipation (cos ϕ ≈ 0, P ≈ 0).
A rheostat dissipates valuable energy as waste heat (I²R loss).
cards.hint: Choke coil controls AC current economically without wasteful power loss.

cards.q: LC Oscillations: Differential equation, frequency, and energy transformation?
cards.a:
Differential equation: d²q / dt² + [ 1 / (L C) ] q = 0.
Oscillation frequency: f = 1 / [ 2π √(L C) ].
Total Energy: E = q² / (2 C) + (1/2) L i² = constant.
cards.hint: Energy continuously oscillates between electric energy in the capacitor and magnetic energy in the inductor.

cards.q: In a series LCR circuit, V_R = 80 V, V_L = 100 V, V_C = 40 V. What is the total applied voltage V?
cards.hint: Top MHT-CET trap! AC voltages are phasors and must be added vectorially, NEVER algebraically.

cards.q: Phasor Diagram: Representation of AC voltage and current?
cards.a: A phasor is a vector rotating counter-clockwise with angular velocity ω about the origin. Its length represents peak value (e₀ or i₀), and its vertical projection represents instantaneous value.
cards.hint: Enables visual geometric addition of alternating quantities of same frequency.

cards.q: What is the frequency of AC mains in India and how many times per second does current reverse?
cards.a:
Frequency: f = 50 Hz (50 cycles per second).
Current reverses direction TWICE per cycle, so it changes direction 100 times per second.
cards.hint: A 50 Hz electric bulb reaches maximum brightness 100 times per second and goes dark 100 times per second!

cards.q: Admittance Y and Susceptance S in AC circuits?
cards.a:
Admittance: Y = 1 / Z (reciprocal of Impedance). SI unit: Siemens (S) or mho.
Conductance: G = R / Z².
Susceptance: S = X / Z².
cards.hint: Admittance measures how easily AC flows through the circuit.

cards.q: Half-Power Frequencies in a series LCR resonant circuit?
cards.a:
Frequencies f₁ and f₂ at which power consumed drops to half its maximum value (P = P_max / 2) and current drops to I_max / √2 ≈ 0.707 I_max.
Bandwidth: Δf = f₂ - f₁ = R / (2π L).
cards.hint: At half-power frequencies, net reactance equals resistance: |X_L - X_C| = R.

cards.q: What happens to the brightness of a bulb connected in series with an inductor across an AC source when an iron core is inserted?
cards.a:
The bulb becomes DIMMER (brightness decreases)!
Inserting an iron core increases inductance L (L ∝ μ_r), which increases inductive reactance X_L = ωL, increasing total impedance Z and decreasing current I.
cards.hint: If connected to a DC source instead, inserting the iron core has zero effect on steady brightness.

cards.q: What happens to the brightness of a bulb connected in series with a capacitor across an AC source when frequency f is increased?
cards.a:
The bulb glows BRIGHTER!
As frequency f increases, capacitive reactance X_C = 1/(2π f C) decreases, reducing total impedance Z and increasing current I.
cards.hint: Higher frequency enables easier conduction through capacitors.

cards.q: Can the voltage across L or C exceed the total applied voltage in a series LCR circuit?
cards.a: YES, absolutely! At or near resonance, V_L = I X_L = Q · V_applied, which can be many times greater than the supply voltage if Q-factor is high.
cards.hint: This voltage magnification phenomenon is called Resonance Voltage Amplification.

cards.q: Form factor and Peak factor for a sinusoidal alternating wave?
cards.a:
Form Factor = RMS value / Average value = (i₀ / √2) / (2 i₀ / π) = π / (2√2) ≈ 1.11.
Peak Factor = Peak value / RMS value = i₀ / (i₀ / √2) = √2 ≈ 1.414.
cards.hint: Form factor 1.11 is used in designing transformer coil winding ratios.

cards.q: If an AC circuit contains an inductor and a capacitor with X_L = 20 Ω and X_C = 20 Ω with R = 0, what is the impedance?
cards.a:
Z = |X_L - X_C| = |20 - 20| = 0 Ω (pure short circuit at resonance!).
Current would theoretically be infinite if driven by an ideal source.
cards.hint: Series LC combination behaves as a pure short circuit at resonance frequency.

cards.q: MHT-CET Trap: An alternating voltage e = 200 sin(100π t + π/3) V is applied. What is its frequency and RMS voltage?
cards.a:
Peak voltage: e₀ = 200 V ⇒ e_rms = 200 / √2 = 100 √2 ≈ 141.4 V.
Angular frequency: ω = 100π rad/s ⇒ Frequency f = ω / 2π = 100π / 2π = 50 Hz.
cards.hint: Do not write 200 V as the RMS voltage; 200 is the peak value!
